title: Equity Risk Premium (CAPE Yield − Real 10-Year Treasury)
revision_note: The CAPE leg comes from Shiller's workbook, whose recent months are revised as S&P finalises earnings; the two FRED legs are not revised after publication.

inputs.label: 10-year Treasury constant-maturity yield, monthly average (FRED GS10)
10-year expected inflation, Cleveland Fed model (FRED EXPINF10YR)

methodology: ERP = (100 ÷ CAPE) − (GS10 − EXPINF10YR), computed per month in Python. A month is emitted only where all three legs report — no forward-fill and no interpolation — so the series begins 1982-01, the first month the Cleveland Fed's expected-inflation model covers.

The equity leg is the CAPE earnings yield: the reciprocal of Shiller's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, which divides the real S&P Composite price by the average of ten years of real earnings. Inverting a P/E gives the earnings the market buys per dollar invested, so 100 ÷ 41 is a 2.4% yield. Ten-year averaging is the point of using CAPE rather than a trailing P/E here: it keeps a single bad earnings year from making stocks look cheap or dear when they are not.

The bond leg is an EX-ANTE real yield: the nominal 10-year Treasury yield minus what investors expected inflation to average over the same ten years, per the Cleveland Fed's model. It is what a bond buyer expected to earn in purchasing power at the moment of purchase, not what they turned out to earn. Chart 5 (Ex-Post Real Short Rate) is the realized counterpart at the short end, and the two are not comparable.

GS10 − EXPINF10YR rather than the directly observed TIPS yield (FRED DFII10), which would need no inflation model but only starts 2003-01. The model-based construction reaches back to 1982 and so covers the disinflation of the 1980s, the 1990s bull market and the dot-com peak — the episodes that make the chart worth drawing. From 2003 onward the two constructions track each other closely.
notes: Values are percentage points. A positive reading means the CAPE earnings yield exceeds the expected real bond yield — stocks are compensating for their extra risk. A negative reading means they are not, on this measure.

This is a valuation-based estimate of the premium investors are being offered, not a forecast of the premium they will earn and not a trading signal. It has been low or negative for long stretches during which equities went on to do well.

Each observation also stores its two legs, `cape_yield` and `real_yield`, so the difference can be decomposed — which side moved matters, since a falling premium means either richer stocks or cheaper real bonds. They are carried in the data file and the JSON export; the chart line, its hover and the CSV export all show the premium alone.
The premium compressed to roughly +0.3pp by August 2026, near the low end of the series' own history — a high CAPE meeting a positive real bond yield, the two forces working the same direction.

Not published (`presentation.publish: false`). The CAPE yield is 1 ÷ CAPE, and CAPE is built from S&P's price and earnings columns in Shiller's workbook. S&P Dow Jones Indices declined free permission on 2026-09-15 and excluded "the P/E values" even from its paid Web Display Agreement; Shiller's own side answered on 2026-09-17 that it licenses nothing and that S&P's wishes govern. Settled rather than pending.
